groups.text: It is currently a clear morning in Berlin-Tempelhof with a temperature of 24 degrees.
With the morning weather set, here is the news.

Severe fuel shortages are hitting Abkhazia during the peak tourist season, a crisis driven by Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian oil and gas facilities. While petroleum products typically come exclusively from Russia, Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze confirmed that private businesses have now supplied fuel from territory controlled by Tbilisi to ease the situation for local residents. This regional instability contrasts with violence in other occupied areas, where a man was killed this morning by an explosion likely planted in a bin on Stoletovsky Avenue in Sevastopol. Unconfirmed reports suggest the victim may be Robert Shahieiev, a deputy commander of the Black Sea Fleet's 4th Separate Submarine Brigade. Meanwhile, in South America, Rosario Central and Corinthians face off tonight at 9:30 Brasília time for the round of 16 in the Libertadores. The match takes place at the Gigante de Arroyito stadium in Argentina.

Ukraine has extended its reach deep into Russia, striking the Gazprom Neftekhim Salavat oil refinery complex overnight. Located some 1,300 kilometers from the Ukrainian border, this facility is one of Russia's largest petrochemical sites and supports the Russian occupation army. Along with the refinery, Ukrainian forces hit a Wildberries warehouse and distribution center in Bashkortostan, continuing a recent pattern of targeting the retail giant's logistics hubs. Meanwhile, Russian forces used jet-powered drones to attack the village of Verbivka in the Kharkiv region this morning. Two strikes on a private house and a non-residential building left five civilians injured. In a different part of the world, students in England, Wales, and Northern Ireland woke up to A-level, T-level, and BTec results released at 8:00 BST today. Those applying to university can now check their status through the Ucas Hub as they navigate grade boundaries and potential appeals.

White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt is stepping down at the end of the month to spend more time with her family following the birth of her second child. The twenty-eight-year-old, who is the youngest person to ever hold the role, will remain a consultant for President Donald Trump. In Germany, political lines are shifting as far-right AfD leader Björn Höcke has offered to support populist Sahra Wagenknecht for state premier in Thuringia, a move that threatens the existing firewall against far-right cooperation. Meanwhile, public health authorities report that heat-related deaths in Germany have reached an estimated 12,500 this year, with the highest tolls seen among those aged eighty-five and older. In a different geopolitical shift, eighty deputies in Madagascar, including independents and former supporters of Andry Rajoelina, have launched a new political platform to structure a majority in support of the current government.

The White House is expanding federal capabilities against foreign cybercrime by authorizing vetted private companies to conduct offensive and intelligence-gathering operations. Managed by the National Coordination Center, this program allows firms to execute cyber surveillance and effects operations targeting transnational criminal organizations under direct federal supervision. To participate, companies must sign contracts with the Department of Justice or Homeland Security, which may require a one million dollar bond that is forfeited if operational requirements are not met. In Nigeria, stakeholders prepare for the August 15 election in Osun State, where Arise Television recently hosted a town hall featuring Governor Ademola Adeleke. Fact-checkers verified that exam performance in the state rose from 33rd to 7th place during his tenure, though evidence remains insufficient regarding his claim of recruiting over 1,500 Amotekun personnel. Meanwhile, the European Broadcasting Union has updated its rules for Eurovision, decreeing that starting in 2027, the contest will not be held in countries at war.

Threat actors are actively exploiting a critical directory traversal vulnerability in VMware vCenter, which allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-59310, was patched by Broadcom on July 29, but the security firm Quirso reports that exploitation began shortly after on August 3. Researchers identified over 360 victim IP addresses across 47 countries, with a heavy concentration in the US, Germany, France, Turkey, and Iran. In separate financial news, Jio Financial Services is selling a 49.9 percent stake in its lending subsidiary, Jio Credit, to Bank of America for 1.9 billion dollars. The deal involves an initial equity stake of 26.5 percent and warrants that can be converted within 18 months. This investment targets a loan book built entirely on secured loans, including business and home loans, with assets under management totaling over 30,000 crore rupees as of June.

In Azad Jammu Kashmir, police say the proscribed Joint Awami Action Committee has abducted eight highway police personnel who were on election duty. Police spokesperson Khawar Ali Shaukat alleges the group attacked security forces and subjected the officers to brutal abuse while threatening their families. Meanwhile, a minibus carrying foreign tourists plunged into a gorge on the Gomis Mta road in Georgia's Guria region on Wednesday. Four people died, including Belarusian citizens, and eleven others were admitted to Batumi Republican Hospital; six of those injured are children. Georgian authorities have launched an investigation into traffic safety violations as deaths from road accidents rose 6.1 percent in 2025 compared with 2023. In a different atmosphere, millions of tourists gathered in Spain on Wednesday evening for the first total solar eclipse visible in Europe in nearly 30 years. While those in the path of totality saw the sun blocked out, one in eight people worldwide glimpsed a partial eclipse.

Yemeni government forces have thwarted a Houthi attack on positions along the al-Mafalis front in Taiz province as military escalation spikes across several governorates. An official from the Tor al-Bahah military axis stated that the 4th Infantry Hashd Brigade repelled the assault, claiming the Houthi militias suffered heavy losses. Government spokesman Waddah al-Dubeish added that air defenses engaged Houthi reconnaissance drones over al-Makha in the southwest. Meanwhile, in the euro area, a new European Central Bank survey shows cash remains the most widely accepted payment method. Acceptance rose to 92 percent of companies with physical points of sale in 2026, up from 90 percent in 2024. While mobile payment acceptance jumped from 36 to 68 percent over that same period, many businesses still value cash for its reliability and privacy. Some firms are pushing digital shifts, with 13 percent introducing self-checkout terminals.
After the headlines, back to the weather.
This afternoon will remain clear with temperatures between 24 and 30 degrees.
And from the weather, a quick look at the calendar.

On your calendar today: Your personal calendar has summer holidays in Berlin and Greifen at seven in the evening. Your work calendar has a meeting with Aaron at two in the afternoon, followed by an AutoML Seminar at four.
Mail worth checking: You have an invitation from Alex at local ai and a payment receipt from PayPal for Valve Corporation. Microsoft also sent an update regarding their terms of service.
And that's it for your personal morning broadcast.
[mature adult voice, intensely emotional, tender, radiant; hold a long breath after Rise] Rise... and shine.
[very very long pause before speaking; then mature adult voice, most emotional, strong, warm, radiant, deeply encouraging; hold a long breath after Rise] Rise... and shine.
